summary: Gives guidelines for applying or extending MPLS and GMPLS protocols and clarifies the IETF working groups' responsibility for them. It targets multi-vendor forums and other standards bodies, and stresses using IETF review procedures. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: If someone wants to change a shared rulebook, they should talk to the group that owns it. This note says who that group is.

questions: how to extend mpls or gmpls
what is the mpls and gmpls change process
what is a requirements statement internet-draft
subtitle: The rulebook for anyone, inside or outside the IETF, who wants to extend MPLS or GMPLS: take it through IETF review first.

tldr.problem: Other forums and standards bodies were publishing non-standard MPLS and GMPLS extensions without IETF review, sometimes presenting them to the IETF as a done deal. The RFC says this can hurt interoperability and add confusion.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a change process: raise the need with the IETF, write a requirements statement Internet-Draft, have a responsible working group evaluate it, and only then do solutions work. The MPLS and CCAMP working groups own the protocols.
tldr.outcome: Changes or extensions to (G)MPLS must not be made by any other mechanism, and the IETF must not endorse RFCs or IANA codepoint allocations that bypass the process. The document does not change the formal IETF standards process.

today: RFC 4929 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 129, June 2007), and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Change Process Is Needed
sections.content:
The IETF develops MPLS and GMPLS on two tracks. MPLS covers packet switched networks. GMPLS applies the MPLS protocols to all types of networks, packet and non-packet. The RFC writes (G)MPLS for both, since GMPLS is by definition a superset of MPLS.

As the protocols became popular, other technology forums began developing, using and publishing non-standard extensions, sometimes without consulting the working groups and then presenting them as a fait accompli. The RFC says this has the potential to hinder interoperability, increase complexity, sow confusion and circumvent the standards process. It builds on RFC 4775, which says major extensions to IETF protocols should only happen through normal IETF processes or in coordination with the IETF.

The IETF cannot force a forum to follow the procedure. Any forum that does not, when it applies for an IANA assignment or IETF publication, will be delayed until the procedure has been completed.
sections.eli5: Imagine a board game where other clubs keep adding their own secret rules. Soon nobody can play together. This note asks everyone to check with the game's owners first.

sections.title: Who the Process Binds
sections.content:
The RFC does not change the formal IETF standards process in RFC 2026 and RFC 2418. It is consistent with RFC 4775 and shows how that applies to (G)MPLS.

The procedures MUST be used when other standards development organizations (SDOs) and forums wish to propose (G)MPLS changes. Inside the IETF they SHOULD be used, unless the responsible Area Director considers the changes non-controversial, for example because they are covered by a working group charter.

The document was the joint work of the IETF Routing Area Directors, the MPLS and CCAMP working group chairs, and the IETF's liaisons to the ITU-T.
sections.eli5: Outside groups have to follow the check-first rule. People inside the IETF should too, unless the change is small and already agreed to be in their job.

sections.title: Who Owns MPLS and GMPLS
sections.content:
Two working groups in the IETF Routing Area develop the technology. The MPLS working group standardizes the base label switching technology and Label Switched Paths (LSPs) over packet and frame-based link technologies. The CCAMP (Common Control and Measurement Plane) working group focuses on GMPLS, with common methods across a broad range of switching technologies.

The RFC assumes these two groups remain the chartered authorities. The IETF may appoint another working group for specific changes. If a group finishes and closes, the IETF will use the non-working group standards track process from RFC 2026 with designated experts. The two groups sometimes split work in ways their charters do not strictly describe, for example for P2MP TE LSPs. Someone proposing a change should choose one group first, but the chairs and Area Directors may redirect the proposal.

Other groups, such as BFD, L2VPN, L3VPN, L1VPN and PWE3, may use (G)MPLS. Where they need changes, their charters and the normal IETF process apply. L1VPN will not develop GMPLS extensions in isolation: its proposals are reviewed and approved by the (G)MPLS working groups. Organizations outside the IETF are covered whether or not they have a formal liaison relationship.
sections.eli5: Two teams look after the rulebook: one for the everyday version and one for the extra-flexible version. If you want a change, you start by talking to one of them.

sections.title: The Change Process Step by Step
sections.content:
Anyone who thinks the existing (G)MPLS protocols will not meet their needs MUST use this process. Changes or extensions MUST NOT be made by any other mechanism, and the IETF MUST NOT endorse RFCs, on any track, or IANA allocations of (G)MPLS codepoints that do not arise from it.

  1. Preliminary investigation (optional). A lightweight, informal way to find out whether the problem has been examined and is in scope. No Internet-Draft is required, but early consultation is RECOMMENDED. It cannot move straight to solutions unless the working group agrees, for example because the problem is minor.
  2. Requirements statement. A requirements statement Internet-Draft MUST be written and introduced to the requirements evaluation working group (REWG) list or the Routing Area list, or via a formal liaison. The responsible Area Director MUST decide whether it will be formally evaluated and deliver a response.
  3. REWG evaluation. The REWG works toward a clear, complete statement of the requirements. The output is either a draft with working group consensus that has passed working group last call, or a rejection.
  4. AD and IESG review. The Area Directors review the finished draft and pass it to the IESG, which also reviews any charter change for the protocol solutions working group (PSWG).
  5. Solutions work. The PSWG works under the normal IETF process.

The possible IETF responses to a requirements statement are: not understood, out of scope, understood but no extension needed, or understood and the IETF wants to develop extensions.
sections.eli5: First you chat about your idea. Then you write down exactly what you need. A group checks it, the bosses sign off, and only then do people work out the actual new rule.

sections.title: Solutions Work and Outside Contributions
sections.content:
Solutions Internet-Drafts may be prepared outside the IETF, for example in another organization, and may be submitted early to help the REWG discuss requirements. But no draft is formally considered a solutions draft until the PSWG has a charter item covering the work and the REWG chairs are confident the requirements are stable.

The IETF makes no guarantee that an externally produced draft will be the basis of the PSWG's solution, but the PSWG MUST consider it using the same open procedures as any individual submission. The source forum is not recommended to keep working on solutions in parallel with the IETF's work, and its implementers and users are strongly encouraged to take part.

The originating SDO should ensure appropriate industry interest, or the IETF MAY discontinue its support. Where a formal liaison exists, the PSWG SHOULD report progress regularly, MUST send the solutions draft to the originator during working group last call, and MUST tell it when the solution is complete.
sections.eli5: Other clubs can offer their own ideas for the new rule, and the group has to read them fairly. But it does not have to pick yours, and you should not build a competing rule on the side.

sections.title: Rejection and Abandonment
sections.content:
Rejecting a requirements statement is called a sensitive matter and MUST be handled with full disclosure and explanation. The reasons listed are:

  • Not understood: discussion continues.
  • Out of scope for the IETF: the IETF MUST NOT stop the authors from working on a solution elsewhere. If (G)MPLS changes are later identified, they must restart the process.
  • No extension needed: the REWG MUST explain how existing protocols meet the requirements and MAY help produce an Applicability Statement or Profiles draft.
  • Insufficient IETF support: the authors may present their solution to the PSWG for possible publication as an Informational or Experimental RFC, and the IETF SHALL NOT block IANA codepoint applications pending that review.
  • Insufficient support from the original requesters: the IETF MUST NOT permit the work elsewhere, endorse the changes or instruct IANA to allocate codepoints.
  • The change would break the technology: a different technology is recommended, and again the IETF MUST NOT permit the work elsewhere.

The rejection must be communicated by the same route the request used, by email copied to an IETF list or by formal liaison response. Rejections and abandonment of a solutions draft may be appealed using the mechanism in RFC 2026. If solutions work is abandoned, work MUST NOT be started in another forum, and any new attempt starts at the top.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the answer is no. The group has to explain why in public and say what you can do next, and you are allowed to ask for the decision to be looked at again.

sections.title: Protecting the Protocols
sections.content:
The (G)MPLS working groups are REQUIRED to protect the architectural integrity of the protocols. They MUST NOT extend the architecture with features that lack general use beyond a specific case, and MUST NOT change it just to make some function more efficient at the expense of simplicity or generality.

Additions must consider interoperability with existing and future versions. The RFC says point solutions and overlapping features are much harder to control with rules and risk affecting the protocol as a whole. The (G)MPLS PSWG is the chartered owner of the protocol while it exists, and all changes or extensions MUST first be reviewed by it.
sections.eli5: The owners keep the rulebook simple and fair for everyone, so they say no to rules that only help one special case.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Requirements statement drafts MUST fully consider the security impact of the proposed features, and solutions drafts MUST consider the impact on the extension and on the existing protocol. The RFC says it introduces no security issues for any (G)MPLS protocol.

It does note that the IETF process itself is at risk from denial of service, and this document might add to that risk. Provided the number of requirements drafts is not unreasonable, there will be no significant impact. The IESG MAY use the rate of arrival of such drafts to detect attacks and SHOULD act on it.

The RFC makes no specific requests to IANA. It assumes IANA keeps to the allocation policies of the (G)MPLS codepoint registries, and that the IETF will not endorse codepoint allocations made outside this procedure.
sections.eli5: The main worry is someone flooding the group with junk requests. If that starts, the bosses can notice the flood and deal with it.
